\chapter{The Core Verbs}
\label{ch:te-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build a Telugu verb as stem plus tense plus person, say why one form covers both \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I will go\textquotedblright{}, give a polite command with -aṇḍi, and explain why \te{ఉండు} has to borrow its negative and \te{తెలుసు} has no person at all.}

Say \te{నాకు} \te{తెలుసు}, name the three slots that built uṇṭānu, veḷtānu and cūstānu, separate it from Chapter 6's \te{నాకు} \te{తెలుగు} \te{వచ్చు} — fact against skill — and recall that \te{ఉండు} switches to lē- to be negated.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[uṇḍu]{\te{ఉండు} (uṇḍu) — \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} and the negative that is a different verb}

\label{lesson:TE-C32-undu}



\begin{quote}
Thirty-one chapters of words. Now the engine room. Telugu glues a verb together one piece at a time, seams showing, and this first verb carries the machine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఉండు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{ఉండు}} — \emph{uṇḍu} — \textbf{to be, to exist, to stay}
\end{quote}

Chapter 5 met it as \textquotedblleft{}to live somewhere.\textquotedblright{} Here it is the verb-machine itself: \textbf{\te{ఉండ్}-} (the stem) + \textbf{-\te{త}-} (tense) + \textbf{-\te{ాను}} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textbf{\te{ఉంటాను}} (\emph{uṇṭānu}), \textquotedblleft{}I stay, I will be.\textquotedblright{}

One form is already in your mouth: \textbf{\te{ఉన్నాను}} (\emph{unnānu}), \textquotedblleft{}I am — right now,\textquotedblright{} the shape hiding inside \emph{bāgunnānu} and \emph{mīru elā unnāru?}

Telugu is alone in this word. Tamil says \textbf{\ta{இரு}} (\emph{iru}), Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಇರು}} (\emph{iru}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ഇരിക്കുക}} (\emph{irikkuka}) — one verb, three sisters. Telugu went its own way, as it did with \emph{lēdu}.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\te{ఉ}} is the standing vowel \emph{u}. \textbf{\te{ండు}} is the retroflex cluster \emph{ṇḍ} with the \emph{u} sign — tongue tip curled back, then released. Both shapes are familiar from Chapter 5.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}be\textquotedblright{} cannot be made negative}]
There is no negative of \emph{uṇḍu}. To say something is \textbf{not} there, Telugu drops the verb and picks up a second one, \textbf{\te{లే}-} (\emph{lē-}) — the root behind Chapter 1's \emph{lēdu}. It takes the very same person-endings:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{who} & \textbf{is} & \textbf{is not} \\
\midrule
I & \emph{unnānu} & \emph{lēnu} \\
he & \emph{unnāḍu} & \emph{lēḍu} \\
it & \emph{undi} & \emph{lēdu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{lēdu} was never a bare word for \textquotedblleft{}no.\textquotedblright{} It is the \textbf{it}-form of a full verb, and you can now run it through its persons.

This is where Telugu parted from its sisters. Tamil negates \emph{iru} with \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} (\emph{illai}), Kannada with \textbf{\ka{ಇಲ್ಲ}} (\emph{illa}), Malayalam with \textbf{\ml{ഇല്ല}} (\emph{illa}) — one shared root, \emph{il-}. Telugu dropped it and grew \emph{lē-} instead.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}uṇḍu\textquotedblright{} — be, exist, stay
  \item the three pieces in order — \textquotedblleft{}uṇḍ … ta … ānu\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}uṇṭānu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair you must switch verbs for — \textquotedblleft{}unnānu … lēnu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three sisters' one verb — \textquotedblleft{}iru … iru … irikkuka\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the three pieces of \emph{uṇṭānu}? (\textbf{Stem, tense, person} — \emph{uṇḍ-}, \emph{-ta-}, \emph{-ānu}.) How do you say \textquotedblleft{}I am not there\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\te{లేను}}, \emph{lēnu} — a different verb entirely.) So what kind of word is \emph{lēdu}? (\textbf{The it-form of the negative verb} \emph{lē-}.) Which root do the other three sisters use, and does Telugu? (\emph{\textbf{il-}}; Telugu does \textbf{not}.) Next: the same machine, tense piece swapped.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veḷḷu]{\te{వెళ్ళు} (veḷḷu) — \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and a tense Telugu refuses to split}

\label{lesson:TE-C32-vellu}



\begin{quote}
You have the three pieces — stem, tense, person. Change only the middle one. That is the whole of Telugu tense, and it has one setting fewer than you would expect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{వెళ్ళు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{వెళ్ళు}} — \emph{veḷḷu} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

Chapter 4 gave it to you as a bare command, \emph{veḷḷu!}, \textquotedblleft{}go!\textquotedblright{} Threaded up it is \textbf{\te{వెళ్తాను}} (\emph{veḷtānu}), and its past is \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళాను}} (\emph{veḷḷānu}), \textquotedblleft{}I went.\textquotedblright{}

Telugu keeps a second go-verb beside it. The family's inherited word for going is \emph{\textbf{pō-}}, and Telugu has it as \textbf{\te{పోవు}} (\emph{pōvu}), \textbf{\te{పోతాను}} (\emph{pōtānu}) — the same verb as Tamil \textbf{\ta{போ}} (\emph{pō}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{പോകുക}} (\emph{pōkuka}) and Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಹೋಗು}} (\emph{hōgu}). So Telugu did not lose the family's word; it gave the everyday job to \emph{veḷḷu}, a verb of its own whose deeper history is best left open.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\te{వె}} is \emph{va} with the short-\emph{e} sign. \textbf{\te{ళ్ళు}} is the retroflex \textbf{\te{ళ}} (\emph{ḷ}) doubled and held — \emph{veḷ-ḷu}, a real catch in the middle. The same doubling is in \emph{nīḷḷu}, Chapter 15's water.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one piece for \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I will go\textquotedblright{}}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{when} & \textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{the middle piece} \\
\midrule
now, or later & \emph{veḷtānu} & \emph{-ta-} \\
already & \emph{veḷḷānu} & \emph{-ā-} \\
this minute & \emph{veḷtunnānu} & \emph{-tunnā-} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Be honest about the first row: \textbf{\te{వెళ్తాను}} means \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} \textbf{and} \textquotedblleft{}I will go.\textquotedblright{} Telugu does not separate habit from future — one piece does both, and context decides. Tamil keeps them apart (\emph{pōgiṟēṉ} against \emph{pōvēṉ}); Telugu merged them.

Having merged them, Telugu needed a way to say \textquotedblleft{}right this minute,\textquotedblright{} and built one out of last lesson's verb. \textbf{\te{వెళ్తున్నాను}} (\emph{veḷtunnānu}) is \emph{veḷ-} plus \textbf{\te{ఉన్నా}-}, the very \emph{unnānu} that means \textquotedblleft{}I am,\textquotedblright{} welded on: literally \textquotedblleft{}going-am-I.\textquotedblright{} The be-verb did not stay a word. It became a piece of every other verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}veḷḷu\textquotedblright{} — go — then \textquotedblleft{}veḷtānu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two meanings of one form — \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I will go\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three times — \textquotedblleft{}veḷtānu … veḷḷānu … veḷtunnānu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the be-verb hiding in the third — \textquotedblleft{}unnānu … veḷtunnānu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many things does \emph{veḷtānu} mean? (\textbf{Two} — \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I will go\textquotedblright{}; Telugu merges habit and future.) What is glued inside \emph{veḷtunnānu}? (\textbf{\te{ఉన్నా}-}, the be-verb — \textquotedblleft{}going-am-I.\textquotedblright{}) Does Telugu have the family's old go-root at all? (\textbf{Yes} — \emph{pōvu}, cousin of \emph{pō}, \emph{pōkuka}, \emph{hōgu}; \emph{veḷḷu} just took the everyday work.) Next: a verb you call by one shape and build on another.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rā]{\te{రా} (rā) — \textquotedblleft{}come!\textquotedblright{}, and the stem it is not built on}

\label{lesson:TE-C32-raa}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Veḷḷu} threads its pieces on without a fuss: the word you call it by is the word you build on. Its partner refuses — and the goodbye you learned in Chapter 4 has been hiding the reason.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{రా}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{రా}} — \emph{rā} — \textbf{come!}
\end{quote}

One syllable: \textbf{\te{ర}} (\emph{ra}) with the long-\emph{ā} sign. It is a whole command on its own, the plainest thing one Telugu speaker can say to another.

Every sister has this verb, and every sister's command-shape drifted somewhere different: Tamil \textbf{\ta{வா}} (\emph{vā}), Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಬಾ}} (\emph{bā}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{വരുക}} (\emph{varuka}), Telugu \textbf{\te{రా}} (\emph{rā}). A \emph{v}, a \emph{b}, an \emph{r} — one old Dravidian come-word, worn three ways, not three separate verbs.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word you call it by is not the word you build on}]
Try to thread endings onto \emph{rā-} and you get nothing anyone says. They attach to \textbf{\te{వచ్చు}} (\emph{vaccu}) instead, which appears as \emph{vast-} once the tense piece arrives:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{వస్తాను}} (\emph{vastānu}) — \textquotedblleft{}I come, I will come\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\te{వచ్చాను}} (\emph{vaccānu}) — \textquotedblleft{}I came\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\te{వస్తున్నాను}} (\emph{vastunnānu}) — \textquotedblleft{}I am coming right now\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

The third one is last lesson's trick again: the be-verb \emph{unnā-} welded onto the stem. Learn this verb as a pair, then — \emph{\textbf{rā}}, and \emph{\textbf{vaccu-}}. Telugu is not odd here; Tamil pairs \emph{vā} with \emph{varu-} and Kannada pairs \emph{bā} with \emph{baru-}, and the building-stems stayed far closer to each other than the commands did.

You have said \emph{vastānu} already. Chapter 4's farewell \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{వస్తాను}} (\emph{veḷḷi vastānu}) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{} — is \emph{veḷḷu} and \emph{vaccu} standing side by side, and that second word is exactly the form above. Chapter 6 used the bare stem too, in \emph{nāku telugu vaccu}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the command — \textquotedblleft{}rā!\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair to learn together — \textquotedblleft{}rā … vaccu-\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vastānu … vaccānu … vastunnānu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the farewell you now understand — \textquotedblleft{}veḷḷi vastānu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which shape do the endings attach to for \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\te{వచ్చు}}, \emph{vaccu-}, never \emph{rā-}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I will come.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Vastānu}.) Which two verbs are standing in \emph{veḷḷi vastānu}? (\textbf{\te{వెళ్ళు}} and \textbf{\te{వచ్చు}} — go, and come back.) Are Tamil \emph{vā}, Kannada \emph{bā} and Telugu \emph{rā} three different verbs? (\textbf{No} — one old come-word, reshaped three ways.) Next: a verb Telugu kept where Tamil replaced it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tinu]{\te{తిను} (tinu) — \textquotedblleft{}to eat,\textquotedblright{} the root Telugu kept}

\label{lesson:TE-C32-tinu}



\begin{quote}
Three verbs in, and every one has been Telugu's own choice. This one is the opposite: the oldest eat-word the family has, still doing plain everyday work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తిను}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{తిను}} — \emph{tinu} — \textbf{to eat}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\te{తి}} is the dental \emph{ta} with the \emph{i} sign; \textbf{\te{ను}} is \emph{nu}, the same shape that ends \emph{nēnu}. Threaded up: \textbf{\te{తింటాను}} (\emph{tiṇṭānu}), \textquotedblleft{}I eat, I will eat,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\te{తిన్నాను}} (\emph{tinnānu}), \textquotedblleft{}I ate.\textquotedblright{}

The inherited Dravidian root is \emph{\textbf{tiṉ-}}, and the family kept it: Kannada \textbf{\ka{ತಿನ್ನು}} (\emph{tinnu}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{തിന്നുക}} (\emph{tinnuka}), Tamil \textbf{\ta{தின்}} (\emph{tiṉ}). But Tamil narrowed its own to chewing and snacking and put an assembled compound, \textbf{\ta{சாப்பிடு}} (\emph{sāppiḍu}), in the everyday slot. Telugu did no such thing. \emph{Tinu} is still simply the word.

\begin{cousinweb}
Build a noun straight off the root and you get \textbf{\te{తిండి}} (\emph{tiṇḍi}) — \textquotedblleft{}food, grub.\textquotedblright{} Native, transparent, and blunt: it is what you feed people, not what you invite them to.

For the invitation Telugu reaches across to Sanskrit: \textbf{\te{భోజనం}} (\emph{bhōjanaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}a meal\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\te{ఆహారం}} (\emph{āhāraṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}food\textquotedblright{}). Both are \textbf{tatsama} loans, taken in whole, and both outrank \emph{tiṇḍi} in politeness without displacing it.

That is Telugu's Sanskrit habit in miniature, and it is worth naming plainly. The verbs at the centre of living — be, go, come, eat — stayed Dravidian. The formal and ceremonial vocabulary layered on top came from Sanskrit. You met the same split in Chapter 1, where the greeting \emph{namaskāram} is Sanskrit while \emph{avunu} and \emph{sarē} are native. Telugu borrowed far more of that top layer than Tamil ever did; it did not borrow the floor.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tinu\textquotedblright{} — eat — then \textquotedblleft{}tiṇṭānu … tinnānu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root the whole family kept — \textquotedblleft{}tinu … tinnu … tinnuka\textquotedblright{}
  \item the native noun and the borrowed one — \textquotedblleft{}tiṇḍi … bhōjanaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four verbs so far — \textquotedblleft{}uṇṭānu … veḷtānu … vastānu … tiṇṭānu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Did Telugu keep the inherited eat-root? (\textbf{Yes} — \emph{tinu}, plain and everyday, where Tamil demoted \emph{tiṉ} and built \emph{sāppiḍu}.) Which word for food is native, and which is borrowed? (\textbf{\te{తిండి}} \emph{tiṇḍi} is native and blunt; \textbf{\te{భోజనం}} \emph{bhōjanaṁ} is Sanskrit and polite.) What is the pattern? (\textbf{Native verbs at the core, Sanskrit vocabulary layered on top} — as with \emph{avunu} against \emph{namaskāram}.) Next: a verb, and the polite ending that fits every verb in this chapter.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cūḍu]{\te{చూడు} (cūḍu) — \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} and the polite ending that fits every verb}

\label{lesson:TE-C32-cuudu}



\begin{quote}
Four bare commands so far — \emph{uṇḍu}, \emph{veḷḷu}, \emph{rā}, \emph{tinu} — and every one is blunt. This verb brings the ending that makes them polite.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చూడు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{చూడు}} — \emph{cūḍu} — \textbf{to see, to look}
\end{quote}

Threaded up: \textbf{\te{చూస్తాను}} (\emph{cūstānu}), \textquotedblleft{}I see, I will see,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\te{చూశాను}} (\emph{cūśānu}), \textquotedblleft{}I saw.\textquotedblright{}

Here the sisters scatter completely. Tamil says \textbf{\ta{பார்}} (\emph{pār}), Kannada \textbf{\ka{ನೋಡು}} (\emph{nōḍu}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{കാണുക}} (\emph{kāṇuka}), Telugu \textbf{\te{చూడు}} (\emph{cūḍu}). Four languages, four unrelated everyday verbs.

And yet the family's oldest seeing-root is right there in all four, sitting in a noun you can point at: \textbf{\te{కన్ను}} (\emph{kannu}, \textquotedblleft{}eye\textquotedblright{}) — Tamil \textbf{\ta{கண்}} (\emph{kaṇ}), Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಕಣ್ಣು}} (\emph{kaṇṇu}), Malayalam \textbf{\ml{കണ്ണ്}} (\emph{kaṇṇ}). Telugu still builds on it: \textbf{\te{కనిపించు}} (\emph{kanipin̄cu}), \textquotedblleft{}to appear, to be visible.\textquotedblright{} Four everyday verbs, one shared eye.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\te{చూ}} is \textbf{\te{చ}} (\emph{ca}) with the \textbf{long-ū} sign — the drawn-out partner of the short \emph{u} ending every verb in this chapter. Hold it: \emph{cū}, not \emph{cu}. \textbf{\te{డు}} is retroflex \emph{ḍa} with that short \emph{u}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -\te{అండి}, the respectful command, on any stem}]
Chapter 8 gave you \textbf{\te{కూర్చోండి}} (\emph{kūrcōṇḍi}), \textquotedblleft{}please sit.\textquotedblright{} Chapter 9 gave you \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} (\emph{kṣamin̄caṇḍi}), \textquotedblleft{}forgive me.\textquotedblright{} That shared \textbf{-\te{అండి}} (\emph{-aṇḍi}) is not baked into those two words. It is a slot, and every verb in this chapter can fill it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{చూడండి}} (\emph{cūḍaṇḍi}) — please look
  \item \textbf{\te{రండి}} (\emph{raṇḍi}) — please come
  \item \textbf{\te{తినండి}} (\emph{tinaṇḍi}) — please eat
  \item \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళండి}} (\emph{veḷḷaṇḍi}) — please go
\end{itemize}

Bare stem for a child or a close friend; stem plus \emph{-aṇḍi} for everyone else. The respect is built the way Chapter 2 built it: \emph{mīru} is a plural standing in for one person, and \emph{-aṇḍi} is that plural now sitting on the verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cūḍu\textquotedblright{} — see, look — then \textquotedblleft{}cūstānu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four sisters' four verbs — \textquotedblleft{}cūḍu … pār … nōḍu … kāṇuka\textquotedblright{}
  \item the eye they all share — \textquotedblleft{}kannu … kaṇ … kaṇṇu … kaṇṇ\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four polite commands — \textquotedblleft{}cūḍaṇḍi … raṇḍi … tinaṇḍi … veḷḷaṇḍi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do the four sisters share an everyday verb for seeing? (\textbf{No} — \emph{cūḍu}, \emph{pār}, \emph{nōḍu}, \emph{kāṇuka}, all different.) What do they share instead? (\textbf{The eye} — \emph{kannu}, \emph{kaṇ}, \emph{kaṇṇu}, \emph{kaṇṇ}.) Make \textquotedblleft{}please eat\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}please come.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Tinaṇḍi}; \emph{raṇḍi}.) Where have you met that politeness before? (\textbf{In \te{మీరు}} — a plural used for one person, now on the verb.) Next: a verb with no room for a person at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[telusu]{\te{తెలుసు} (telusu) — \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} the verb with no room for a person}

\label{lesson:TE-C32-telusu}



\begin{quote}
Five verbs, and every one ended on \emph{-ānu}, the piece that means \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} The last verb of the chapter has no such piece — and Chapter 6 already handed you the sentence it makes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తెలుసు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{తెలుసు}} — \emph{telusu} — \textbf{it is known}
\end{quote}

Not \textquotedblleft{}to know\textquotedblright{} in the English sense. It comes from \textbf{\te{తెలియు}} (\emph{teliyu}), \textquotedblleft{}to become clear, to be apparent\textquotedblright{} — a thing \emph{telusu}-es to you the way a shape resolves out of fog. Its negative is \textbf{\te{తెలియదు}} (\emph{teliyadu}), \textquotedblleft{}it is not known.\textquotedblright{}

Tamil has the exact cousin, \textbf{\ta{தெரி}} (\emph{teri}). The other two sisters picked different words — Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಗೊತ್ತು}}, \emph{gottu}, Malayalam \textbf{\ml{അറിയാം}}, \emph{aṟiyām} — but all four build the sentence the same way, which is the point of this lesson.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no person on the verb, so the person moves}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుసు}.} — \emph{nāku telusu} — \textquotedblleft{}I know.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\te{తెలుసు}} never changes shape. Only the little dative word in front of it moves:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the knower} & \textbf{the sentence} \\
\midrule
I & \emph{nāku telusu} \\
you & \emph{nīku telusu} \\
he & \emph{ataniki telusu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five verbs put the person in the last piece, which is why \emph{nēnu} could be dropped. Here there is no such piece, so the dative word is the one thing you \textbf{cannot} drop. Telugu treats knowing as something that \textbf{happens to} you, not something you do — and Tamil builds it identically, \emph{enakkut teriyum}.

Now the distinction Chapter 6 could not yet draw. \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుగు} \te{వచ్చు}} uses \emph{vaccu}, \textquotedblleft{}comes\textquotedblright{} — Telugu \textbf{comes to} you, and that is a \textbf{skill}, a language you can actually use. \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుసు}} is a \textbf{fact} you hold. Two dative sentences, two verbs, two kinds of knowing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}telusu\textquotedblright{} — it is known — from \textquotedblleft{}teliyu\textquotedblright{}, to become clear
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāku telusu\textquotedblright{} — I know
  \item three knowers, one verb — \textquotedblleft{}nāku … nīku … ataniki telusu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the five that carried the person — \textquotedblleft{}uṇṭānu, veḷtānu, vastānu, tiṇṭānu, cūstānu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{telusu} mean underneath \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{It is clear, it is apparent} — from \emph{teliyu}.) Which piece is missing from it? (\textbf{The person} — so the knower sits in the dative instead.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I know.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nāku telusu}.) What is the difference from \emph{nāku telugu vaccu}? (\emph{\textbf{Vaccu\emph{ marks a skill\textbf{, \emph{telusu} marks a fact.) Name the three slots one last time, with a verb in them. (}Stem, tense, person\textbf{ — \emph{veḷ} + \emph{-ta-} + \emph{-ānu}.) And what has no negative of its own? (}\te{ఉండు}\textbf{ — Telugu switches to \emph{lē-}.)}}}}
\end{tcolorbox}
